processes.description: A dated credit report on counterparty exposure is produced and Darron Giron forwards it, usually the same day, under a subject such as "Credit Report--2/22/01", with occasional pendings lists. Recipients mostly read it. Sometimes reports go out late or in a catch-up batch after an absence. Later rounds raise questions about content: a list missing the transport positions, and whether figures are quantities at price or calculations.
steps: The credit report for the business day is generated with its date in the title.
The distributor checks the report arrived and is the right date.
The report is forwarded to the standing recipient list.
Recipients review exposure and raise questions on missing positions or how figures are derived.
Missed days are resent together when the distributor returns or systems recover.

stalls.summary: Distribution was delayed by systems issues on the day the report should have gone out.
Reports pile up during the distributor's absence and are resent days later in a batch, so readers get stale exposure figures, for example the 3/13, 3/14 and 3/16 reports all forwarded on 3/19.
Report content is incomplete or unclear to readers: a position list leaves out transport positions, and a reader has to ask whether figures are quantities at price or calculations.

automation.approach: Schedule the credit report to publish and email itself to the distribution list once the daily run completes, with a check that the report date matches the business day and an alert when the run fails, so nothing waits on one person forwarding it. Add a short legend stating which position types are included and how figures are calculated.
automation.rationale: The manual part is a daily check-and-forward that one person carries; a short checklist (confirm date, confirm all position types including transport, send, log late days) keeps it consistent when someone covers and reduces the content questions that follow.

work_estimate.rationale: The trail shows a dated report forwarded with little beyond the email itself; hands-on work is confirming the report ran and carries the right date, opening it, and on some days checking position coverage or answering a figures question. That is a few minutes per round, more when systems fail or positions are missing.

processes.description: Traders or desk heads ask for new EnronOnline products (a Super Peak 5x8 product, hourly products for hours ending 12-20), and operations and EOL staff define the product wording, availability hours, the index each product maps to, and the books traders log in with. Draft product content is circulated for approval or comment, schedulers are briefed on how the new products are ticketed, and product lists are assigned to traders and later revisited in a second pass.
steps: A desk requests a new EOL product and a target launch, such as by bid week.
EOL staff draft the product description, hours and terms.
Operations is asked to approve or comment on the product wording.
The index for the product is mapped to the EOL indexes and books are set for trader log-in.
Products are assigned to traders and the list is reviewed again.
Schedulers and Sitara users are briefed on how the new deals flow and are ticketed.

stalls.summary: Product set-up waits on missing mapping detail: EOL staff have to ask which index should map to the EOL indexes.
The product-to-trader assignment needs rework, with a second pass on the EOL product list weeks after the first.
Downstream deal capture is not set up cleanly at launch: Sitara and EOL staff had to be pressed to add comments, and schedulers needed separate briefing on the new products.

automation.approach: Use a standard product request form that captures product wording, delivery hours, index mapping, book and trader assignment and the approver before set-up starts, and route it through a fixed approval sequence that notifies schedulers and Sitara users on launch.
automation.rationale: Delays and rework come from details that surface late (index mapping, books, trader lists, ticketing comments); a request template gathers them up front, while product design and approval remain judgement calls.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round involves drafting or reviewing product wording and hours, working out the index mapping, setting books and assigning products to traders, and briefing schedulers. Those are reasoning and set-up tasks taking up to an hour typically, longer for multi-product launches; only the collection and notification parts lend themselves to tooling.

processes.description: Each month a coordinator (Shari Mao, James Scribner, Suzanne Nicholie) sends the Hours Survey or activity driver survey with instructions, asking managers to record hours and activities for the month, often in a database or attached spreadsheet, by a stated deadline such as end of day Wednesday, April 5th. Reminders follow on the due date. Separately, team members report absences and vacation to whoever keeps their time, and staff are asked which commercial team they supported and in what share.
steps: The coordinator sends the monthly hours or activity survey with instructions and a due date.
Managers collect hours and activities from their team, sometimes using a provided spreadsheet.
Staff report absences, vacation and travel to the time keeper.
Survey responses or the completed file are entered or returned.
The coordinator chases late responses on and after the deadline.
Figures such as ATEs are checked and corrections returned before the data feeds the cost model.

stalls.summary: Responses come in late: after the deadline passed very few had returned the survey, and reminders go out on the due date itself.
Time entry is blocked by missing system access, so a manager has to go back later to enter his group's time.

contradictions.summary: Suzanne Nicholie is named the primary Hours Survey contact, yet survey requests and instructions come from Shari Mao and James Scribner as well, leaving it unclear who owns collection.

automation.approach: Replace the emailed survey attachments with one standing time and activity form per month, pre-filled with each person's team and prior month's split, with automatic reminders before the deadline and a completion report for the coordinator. Absence and vacation notes go into the same form instead of free-text emails.
automation.rationale: Each round restates the same instructions and collects the same fields; a fixed template with prefilled data reduces entry and chasing, while managers still confirm their team's allocation.

work_estimate.rationale: A round involves preparing and attaching the survey and instructions, managers compiling hours and activities for their team, entering them in the database or spreadsheet, and the coordinator checking figures such as ATEs. Simple absence notices take little; full team surveys take much longer.
